nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Strategy-focused baseball simulation: manage a team through a pennant race, set tactics and edit teams freely, rather than controlling batting and pitching directly.
dossier: ASCII's baseball simulation, which stood out among the many 1988 baseball games for its emphasis on strategy, a realistic pennant race and highly flexible team editing. It evolved from the earlier 'Best Nine', and added extra innings up to the 12th. Player names are parodies of real ones, and magazines printed their own data and the real names for readers. The in-game music uses real teams' cheering songs. It supports ASCII's Turbo File for external saves. The first shipment was small and it stayed scarce, so a 'Shin Data' edition with mid-1988 data followed in October. This was the start of a long-running series.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A management simulation run through Japanese menus, standings and player data.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: Supports ASCII's Turbo File for external save data.

gameplay_summary: Grappling-arm platformer: unable to jump, swing and pull your way through stages with a bionic wire arm, picking areas on an overworld map while avoiding enemy convoys, to rescue Super Joe and stop a revived Hitler's project.
dossier: Capcom's console game built on its arcade Top Secret, but a different, larger game using the same grappling mechanic. The hero can't jump at all. Everything from crossing gaps to climbing ledges is done by firing, swinging from and reeling in the wire of his bionic arm. A helicopter overworld map lets you choose areas non-linearly, but enemy trucks move with you, and getting caught forces an overhead fight. Stages give equipment needed elsewhere. The Japanese original is openly about a resurrected Hitler and Nazi forces, which the NES localization renamed and removed.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The swinging action is visual, but story and in-game messages are Japanese; how much they guide progress isn't documented.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Bionic Commando (1988).
japanese_version_notes: The Japanese version keeps the Nazi references and Hitler by name; the NES version removed the Nazi imagery and renamed him Master-D.

gameplay_summary: Romantic-comedy adventure based on Rumiko Takahashi's manga: as Godai, wander the boarding house and town, stay in Kyoko's good books, fend off the residents' interference, and uncover the secret she is hiding.
dossier: Bothtec's Famicom version of Micro Cabin's 1986 computer adventure based on Rumiko Takahashi's Maison Ikkoku. The story is original but draws on the manga's early chapters. As the luckless Yusaku Godai, you try to win over manager Kyoko Otonashi while the eccentric residents get in the way. The real goal, finding something the game requires and learning Kyoko's secret, isn't obvious if you start blind, and annoying Yotsuya can even get Godai killed. Like the manga's Godai, you wander the house and town and are always short of money. The original saved in the toilet and ended with a financial statement that usually showed a debt. The Famicom version follows that computer game, though how closely isn't detailed.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A dialogue-heavy adventure whose goal isn't spelled out; reading Japanese is essential.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: High-speed side-scrolling platformer: as child star Kakefu-kun, run and leap across a dangerous land collecting seven medicinal herbs to cure an ailing king, with the ending decided by how fast you finish.
dossier: Vic Tokai's celebrity platformer starring Kakefu-kun, the child actor famous for impersonating Hanshin slugger Masayuki Kakefu. In the tiny East African kingdom of Pokonyokkori, King Pokonyokkori V has fallen ill, and only seven herbs from the hazardous Shibireta Federal Republic can cure him. Kakefu-kun takes it on during his summer holiday. As the title (Jump Heaven, Speed Hell) suggests, it's all about momentum jumps and running fast. The ending changes with your clear time, and the good ending needs every stage cleared within three hours. It's very hard: GameCenter CX called it harder than Takahashi Meijin's Adventure Island.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Platform action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Kid Kool (1990).
japanese_version_notes: The hero is Kakefu-kun, the likeness of child actor Kenji Sagara; the NES version renamed him Kid Kool.

gameplay_summary: Floaty puzzle-platformer prequel to The Tower of Druaga: as the priestess Ki, float up through the tower's floors by holding jump, avoiding every enemy without any attack, and grabbing each floor's key to reach the exit.
dossier: Game Studio's third Babylonian Castle Saga game, a prequel to The Tower of Druaga. Ishtar gives the priestess Ki a tiara that turns courage into lightness, and she climbs Druaga's tower to recover the Blue Crystal Rod. She has no attack, so each floor is about dodging enemies, getting the key and reaching the door. Hold jump and she rises until she hits something, release to fall, and her movement has heavy inertia. Bumping her head makes her crouch, which is sometimes needed to let enemies pass overhead. The system is borrowed almost directly from Atari's Major Havoc (its codename was 'Minor Havoc'). Dying on an enemy removes it on the retry, and continues are unlimited. Floor 60 brings the story's bleak ending, and special floors run to 100.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Precision platforming with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Team dodgeball: lead your squad in an expedition against national teams whose players each have names and stats, beat rivals in two-player matches, or play a free-for-all battle royale for up to four.
dossier: Technos Japan's Kunio-kun dodgeball game, a refined version of its 1987 arcade original that does much more with it. Every player on each international team has a name and specialities, and a life gauge that drains when hit. A one-player expedition takes you around the world, two-player versus pits teams against each other, and a free-for-all mode lets up to four people fight within one team until one is left. It became a forerunner of competitive sports games and helped make Technos and Kunio-kun famous. It's still well regarded and holds its value on the used market.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Sports action; team and player names are Japanese but not needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Super Dodge Ball (1989).

gameplay_summary: Vertical platformer sequel to Bubble Bobble: as Bubby, fire rainbows that act as weapons and stairs, climbing each round before the rising water catches you, across a chain of themed islands.
dossier: Taito's Famicom port of the 1987 arcade sequel to Bubble Bobble, developed by Disco. It was originally announced for Disk System in early 1988 before moving to cartridge. Bubby (and Bobby) set out to free the Rainbow Islands from the Dark Shadow behind the first game's trouble. Rainbows shot sideways trap or crush enemies and double as platforms to climb. Each round has to be climbed before the sea rises and drowns you, and each island has its own theme and tougher enemies. The arcade game's first-world tune resembles 'Over the Rainbow' from The Wizard of Oz. The Famicom version keeps an arrangement of it, while the North American NES release replaced it.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Platform action with Japanese and English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Rainbow Islands (1991).
japanese_version_notes: Keeps the 'Over the Rainbow'-like main theme that the North American NES release replaced; level designs are the same.

gameplay_summary: Overhead tank shooter: as Ralf Jones, drive a lone tank from the Normandy landings to Berlin, destroying big guns and enemy tanks to stop Nazi Germany's giant brain computer.
dossier: SNK's Famicom game arranged from its 1985 arcade T.A.N.K. In 1944, with Germany close to collapse, Eisenhower learns that a giant brain computer, 'THINK TANK', is being built in Berlin. He calls Ralf Jones (the Ikari hero) out of the Rockies to land ahead at Normandy. Ralf clears the Big Cannon blocking the landing teams, beats the Big Tank, and pushes on alone to destroy the unfinished computer. It's an overhead tank shooting game. The Japanese version names the enemy outright as Nazi Germany, with its flags, swastikas and lines like 'Heil Hitler', which the NES release removed.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Overhead shooting; the story text is flavour.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Iron Tank: The Invasion of Normandy (1988).
japanese_version_notes: The enemy is explicitly Nazi Germany, with Nazi flags, swastikas and 'Heil Hitler' lines; the NES version changed them to unnamed 'enemies of the United Forces' and blanked the flags.

gameplay_summary: Three Kingdoms strategy: as one of six warlords from AD 200, issue a limited number of written orders each turn to develop and expand, and fight semi-automatic battles with formations to unify China.
dossier: Namco's Three Kingdoms strategy game, developed by Tose. Starting in January of AD 200, you're a warlord aiming to unify China. The strategic side limits how many commands you can issue through written orders, and battles are fought semi-automatically by units you arrange into formations. Before the game starts, a 'hero type' personality quiz assigns your ruler from Liu Bei, Liu Zhang, Sun Quan, Cao Cao, Ma Teng and Yuan Shao. There are only a few questions and one pattern, so after a couple of tries you can easily pick the ruler you want.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Strategy menus, the personality quiz and reports are all Japanese text.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Kung fu action-fighting hybrid: side-scrolling exploration with five dragon warriors, then one-on-one bouts using the Shingan system of targeting marked high, mid and low points, plus transformations and magic powers.
dossier: Culture Brain's second Famicom Hiryuu no Ken. It keeps the series' 'Shingan' fighting system, where circles mark attack and defence points high, mid and low, and adds transformations, magic power and a much stronger story uniting five dragon warriors. Stages now scroll freely in either direction, there's a level system, and you can get a password at any time. All characters share one health pool, so swapping in a fresh fighter doesn't help when you're near death. There's an easy kids' mode and a 'mania' mode where some enemies can't be identified without meeting conditions, and only the mania mode shows the true ending. An 'anime RPG' mode replaces bouts with command choices, and a versus mode was used for a national tournament.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The fighting is visual, but the story, the anime RPG mode commands and the password are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: ja.wikipedia says this game was reworked for North America as Flying Warriors (NES; the NES list dates it February 1991), using Hiryuu no Ken III's graphics with remade stages. Only that one source links the two, so the pairing is low-confidence.
japanese_version_notes: Per ja.wikipedia, the North American Flying Warriors has faster enemies, added instant-death pits, a limited number of continues and American-comic character designs, and borrows the next game's graphics with remade stage layouts.

gameplay_summary: Officially licensed 'realistic' baseball with real NPB teams and players: two-press pitching with timing control, fully manual fielding from a catcher's-eye view, and a catch button for every fielding play.
dossier: VAP's ambitious post-Famista baseball game, the first baseball game in Japan, on any platform, officially licensed by NPB with real team and player names. That makes it the only console baseball game with the Hankyu Braves and Nankai Hawks as active teams under their real names. Every game is played at the then-new Tokyo Dome, also a first for a real ballpark. Its pursuit of realism makes the controls notoriously demanding. Pitching takes two presses whose timing sets the height, with d-pad mashing in between for breaking balls. Fielding is fully manual from a ground-level view behind the catcher, so fly balls disappear and you follow their shadow and sound. Miss the catch button and the ball always drops, and a harsh buzzer marks each out.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Baseball is universal; player names are in hiragana and katakana, but the challenge is the controls, not the text.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Icon-command archaeological adventure in Chichen Itza: search the Mayan ruins for the missing Professor Imes, the Temple of the Sun and its Sun Key, with time-of-day and light RPG elements in the console version.
dossier: Compile's Famicom adaptation of Nihon Falcom's 1986 PC adventure Asteka II, directed by Masayuki Kato with a scenario by Tsuneyuki Miyamoto. It's set in the real ruins of Chichen Itza. You and the professor's daughter, both named by you, search for archaeologist Professor Imes, who vanished while hunting the legendary Sun Key, and for the hidden Temple of the Sun. The original was advanced for its time, with icon commands and a concept of time. The Famicom version reworks it into a more story-driven game with new music and RPG elements. Its land and the golden pedestal also turn up in Falcom's Ys.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — An adventure game built on Japanese descriptions and dialogue; the icons help, but clues need reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Tombs & Treasure (1991).

gameplay_summary: Room-by-room action puzzle: as Lolo, collect every Heart Framer in each room by pushing blocks and turning enemies into eggs, opening the treasure chest to clear it, across 128 rooms laid out in a 16×8 grid.
dossier: HAL's Famicom Eggerland, billed on the box as 'the ultimate puzzle game'. Prince Lolo travels King Egger's realm to rescue Princess Lala. Each room is a single-screen puzzle: collect all the Heart Framers to open the chest, then grab its contents. Most rooms have enemies, so you push Emerald Framers to block them, use the terrain, and fire Egg Shots from certain hearts to turn enemies into eggs. Eggs can be pushed, used as shields, or floated on water as rafts. Shoot an egg again and it's knocked off-screen and respawns. There are 128 rooms in a 16×8 grid. Their connections are simpler than in earlier games, but hint rooms and real brain-teasers remain.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Pure puzzle play with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. The NES Adventures of Lolo games belong to the same series but are separate identities.

gameplay_summary: Behind-the-pitcher baseball in the Moero!! Pro Yakyuu style: control pitch location up, down and sideways, swing to match, and play single games or a pennant race.
dossier: Jaleco's 1988 sequel to its huge hit Moero!! Pro Yakyuu (Bases Loaded), developed by Tose. The series is known for its TV-broadcast presentation: a camera behind the pitcher, so pitches can be thrown high and low as well as side to side and the batter adjusts the swing to match, plus voice synthesis and near-real player names. Like the first game it offers single games and a pennant race. The NES release uses a fictional twelve-team league.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Baseball is universal; player names are Japanese but not needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Bases Loaded II: Second Season (1990).

gameplay_summary: Point-and-click adventure with action-RPG fights: as Ramenman, move and investigate by clicking arrow icons, level up by defeating foes in fighting-game-style duels, and master the seven masters' secret arts.
dossier: Bandai's game of Yudetamago's Kinnikuman spin-off about the kung fu master Ramenman, released alongside the 1988 anime. Three villains, Kinryu, Hakuryu and Kokuryu, have escaped from Chikinmon seeking revenge on the Seven Masters, and Ramenman has to learn their seven secret arts and the supreme fist to stop them. You move and investigate by clicking arrow icons on screen, adventure-style. Defeating enemies earns experience and levels, and fights play out like a fighting game, where you drain the opponent's health bar. The cast and story order differ from the manga. Continuing uses a hiragana password.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — An adventure built on Japanese dialogue and investigation, with a hiragana password.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Money-themed game from SOFEL; the sources give no gameplay detail.
dossier: A SOFEL release, published on cartridge (product code SFL-MY) on August 10, 1988, the same day as Moero!! Pro Yakyuu '88 and Fight!! Ramenman. There's no ja.wikipedia article for it in the research snapshot and FamiWiki has no description, so even the genre is unconfirmed by the sources consulted; the title suggests an economic or investment theme. The primary genre recorded here is provisional.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A money- or economy-themed game would presumably be text-heavy in Japanese; not confirmed.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Action-investigation parody: as Kaku-san and Suke-san, question townspeople and rough up villains for clues across world cities, switching to helpers like the ninja Yashichi to gather evidence, then have Lord Mito pass judgement.
dossier: Sunsoft's second Mito Koumon game, which drops the first game's period setting for all-out parody. The traitorous Mito retainer Ando, jailed after the first game, escapes abroad, and Lord Mito's party chases him around the world. In America he's 'Buffalo Django', and the trail goes through Germany, Italy, India and China to Hawaii, where he's become King Kamehameha and is popular with the locals. Along the way they meet Leonardo da Vinci and Siddhartha, and vampires. Play follows the series formula. As Kaku-san or Suke-san you question people and beat villains until they talk, filling a clue gauge before Lord Mito passes judgement. Items summon helpers such as Hachibei or the ninja Yashichi and Ogin, who can reach places and information the main heroes can't. Running out of time or falling into water is a constant risk.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Investigation by questioning townspeople; the clues are Japanese dialogue.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Multi-genre action across nine stages: mostly belt-scrolling brawling as Billy West, plus two light-gun shooting stages and two front-view jeep driving stages, to rescue Annabelle from the crime boss Gordon.
dossier: Konami's genre-mixing action game. In the Japanese story, Billy West is a Vietnam veteran living quietly in the countryside, and his romance with Annabelle, a wealthy heiress, is opposed by everyone around them. A mysterious syndicate led by Gordon kidnaps her to lure him out. Most of the nine stages are belt-scrolling brawling, with punches, kicks, jump kicks and dropped weapons like a knife, club and whip. Stages 2 and 7 are first-person gun stages, playable with the Famicom light gun, and stages 4 and 5 are front-view jeep driving. A practice mode lets you rehearse each style. The Famicom original is noticeably easier than the NES Bayou Billy, which was reworked extensively.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action throughout; the Japanese story text is not needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as The Adventures of Bayou Billy (1989), an altered version.
japanese_version_notes: Gun stages support the Kōsenjū light gun. Compared with the NES version it's easier, has a health gauge for the jeep, and differs in audio, visuals and story framing.

gameplay_summary: Soccer game from Data East; the sources give no gameplay detail.
dossier: Data East's soccer game, developed with Sakata SAS (who also worked on Data East's Karnov and Jinguji Saburo cartridges) and released on August 12, 1988 (product code DFC-WN). There's no ja.wikipedia article for it in the research snapshot and FamiWiki has no description, so its teams, modes and controls aren't documented in the sources consulted.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — A soccer game; presumably playable without reading, though not confirmed.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Card-driven Dragon Ball RPG-adventure: move Goku around board-game-style maps by playing cards, face random 'fate' events and card battles, and solve command-menu adventure scenes on the way to Piccolo's Dark Castle.
dossier: Bandai's second Famicom Dragon Ball game, developed by Tose. It switched from the first game's action to the card-based RPG system that later games kept. On the map you play one of your cards and move as many spaces as it has stars, and each move triggers an event: a fight, training or recovery. Card contents also decide your attacks in battle, and wins give training points (experience). At each destination a command-select adventure section begins, where you talk to people and examine things to solve the situation. The goal follows the manga, defeating the revived Demon King Piccolo, but the story is heavily rearranged with many original enemies. It leans more on adventure than later entries and has the series' most wrong-command game-over traps.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — The card system is learnable, but the adventure sections and their game-over traps depend on reading Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: F1 racing with split-screen two-player: race against the computer or a friend on a horizontally divided 3D screen, tuning your machine, across several circuits.
dossier: Arc System Works' first released game: a Namco-published Famicom take on Namco's 1987 arcade Final Lap. The arcade original was famous for eight-player linked cabinets on Suzuka and for 'rubber-band' catch-up. The Famicom version is mostly its own game, with more tracks and simpler handling. Its talking point was a top-and-bottom split screen that put two 3D race views on one TV, which was striking at the time. There's a one-player mode against the computer and two-player versus, and you can tune the car.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Racing; the tuning menus are the only text and can be learned by trial.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Turn-based military strategy: as Red Star or Blue Moon, spend funds to build infantry, vehicles, aircraft and ships at captured factories and ports, and win each map by taking the enemy HQ or wiping out its army.
dossier: The first game in Intelligent Systems' Wars series, known abroad as Advance Wars, produced by Gunpei Yokoi. Red Star and Blue Moon face off across fifteen maps, plus ending maps unlocked by clearing them. Each turn brings funds, more from captured cities, to build units at factories, seaports and airports. There are 16 unit types: two infantry, eight vehicles, four aircraft and two ships. You win by capturing the enemy HQ or destroying everything. There's no fog of war, and the computer's two strength settings only change how much damage it takes. Two players can alternate on one console. Clearing the final map plays a staff roll styled as a military parade. Save data is notoriously easy to lose, and shipments were small for how popular it was.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The maps and units are visual, but menus and unit names are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Sengoku unification strategy: pick a daimyo and allocate his stats, then work through yearly phases of war, domestic policy, movement and diplomacy, using court ranks and vassalage as well as force, before old age ends your reign.
dossier: Irem's Sengoku strategy game, developed by Tamtex. You choose a daimyo and distribute ability points at the start, which shapes your whole strategy and makes each province a different challenge. Brute force isn't the only route: court ranks and a vassal system let rival lords submit to you. Generals' stats are hidden, and in battle you only give broad orders. Morale collapse decides fights as much as numbers, and losing a field battle sends the defender into a siege against castles of fixed strength, with Odawara and Ishiyama Honganji nearly impregnable. Each year runs through phases. Weather, famine, ikko-ikki uprisings and nanban trade affect income, and snowbound regions can only campaign in certain seasons. There's no succession, so your daimyo dies in a set year whatever your progress. The 1555 start was chosen because the developer was a Saito Dosan fan. The opening visuals and music are standouts.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A historical strategy game run entirely through Japanese menus, names and events.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Pinball video game with mahjong elements, for one to four alternating players; the sources give no detail of its tables.
dossier: Coconuts Japan's pinball game, developed by Soft Machine. The ja.wikipedia master list says it mixes pinball with mahjong elements, and FamiWiki lists alternating play for up to four. A North American version, Super Sushi Pinball, was announced by CSG Imagesoft and shown at CES 1989 with sushi theming, but was never released. The Video Game History Foundation later found a prototype. The sources don't describe the table layout or how the mahjong side works.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Pinball with English text; the mahjong element may be easier to follow with some mahjong knowledge.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. A North American release as Super Sushi Pinball was announced but cancelled.

gameplay_summary: Alternating action: side-scrolling platform stages on foot alternate with side-scrolling shooter stages riding a cyborg beast, as you fight a machine empire to rescue a princess, with shops, power-ups and multiple endings.
dossier: Atlus's action game for Hudson, set in a near-future retelling of the Urashima Taro folk tale. Ken Urashima has to defeat Goruza's machine-beast empire and rescue Princess Otohime XVIII of the Ryugu kingdom. Ordinary stages are side-scrolling platform action, and some switch to side-scrolling shooting, which was unusual for the time. You ride a cyborg beast after odd-numbered stages, and each ride raises your maximum life. On foot, weapons and special items come from the Dog Sage's rooms or from shop doors that take E balls as currency. In the air, S and P capsules raise speed and firepower. Multiple endings were also unusual for 1988. The NES Xexyz swaps the Urashima framing for a post-apocalyptic year-2777 story.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The action is visual, but shops, the Dog Sage's rooms and information text are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Xexyz (1990).
japanese_version_notes: The story is based on the Urashima Taro legend (Ken Urashima rescuing Princess Otohime XVIII); the NES version reworked it into a sci-fi plot with the hero Apollo.

gameplay_summary: Action RPG: as the red-haired swordsman Adol, explore the island of Esteria, collecting the Books of Ys and battling monsters on the way to Darm Tower.
dossier: Victor's Famicom version of Nihon Falcom's 1987 action RPG, developed by Advance Communication. Adol Christin comes to the storm-locked island of Esteria and, guided by the fortune-teller Sara, seeks the Books of Ys, which hold the history of a lost kingdom. It's the first half of a two-part story completed by Ys II. FamiWiki notes that this port changes the original more than any other version. The overworld layout is reworked, Adol walks and regenerates more slowly, the level cap rises from 10 to 24, a side quest is required before the Mines, Darm Tower is redesigned and can be left freely, some bosses fight differently, and beating Dark Fact gives an item leading to a second fight with the real Dark Fact instead of the sixth book.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Combat is simple, but progress depends on Japanese townspeople's hints and the story.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: Differs substantially from other versions of Ys: reworked overworld, level cap 24, slower walking and regeneration, a required side quest for the Mines, a redesigned Darm Tower, and an extra true fight with Dark Fact.

gameplay_summary: Badminton game for one or two players, the Famicom's only badminton title; the sources give no further gameplay detail.
dossier: VAP's badminton game, developed by Pax Softnica, and the only badminton game on the Famicom, as both the ja.wikipedia master list and FamiWiki note. FamiWiki lists one or two players and English in-game text. There's no ja.wikipedia article for it in the research snapshot, so its modes, players and controls aren't documented in the sources consulted.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — A sports game with English text per FamiWiki; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Shogi game from SNK; the sources give no gameplay detail.
dossier: SNK's 1988 release, developed by Alpha Denshi. The title 'Famicom Meijinsen' refers to the Meijin title tournament of professional shogi, and the census records it as a shogi game. There's no ja.wikipedia article for it in the research snapshot and FamiWiki has no description, so its modes, computer strength and features aren't documented in the sources consulted.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Shogi pieces are marked in kanji and menus are Japanese; players who already know shogi can manage.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Verb-and-pointer graphic adventure: as Dave, choose two classmates with different skills and switch between all three to explore Dr. Fred's mansion and rescue Sandy, with puzzles and endings depending on the team.
dossier: Jaleco's Japan-only port of Lucasfilm Games' Maniac Mansion, separate from the American NES version. After a meteor lands nearby, the once-kindly Dr. Fred withdraws into strange experiments, and when cheerleader Sandy disappears into his house, her boyfriend Dave brings two friends to get her out. You pick verbs and point at things, switching between the three characters. Who you bring changes how puzzles are solved and how the game ends. Jaleco redrew the cast in a cute style, shrank the rooms and used flip-screens. It adapts details for Japan (a postbox is added, dimes and quarters become 10- and 100-yen coins), and the western hint poster is missing, which makes the dark-humoured, trap-filled game even harder. Saving needs a password of over 100 characters.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A verb-driven adventure with Japanese commands and dialogue, no hint poster, and instant-death traps.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. The NES Maniac Mansion is a separate version developed by Lucasfilm Games and Realtime Associates, not this Jaleco port.
japanese_version_notes: Japan-only Jaleco port, with cute redrawn characters, shrunken rooms, flip-screen movement, a 100+ character password, a postbox and yen coins. It has no hint poster.

gameplay_summary: Seoul-Olympics multi-sport game: represent a chosen country across a wide range of events, from fencing and taekwondo to swimming, archery and the horizontal bar, with button-mashing and timing controls.
dossier: Konami's 1988 Olympic-year follow-up to Hyper Olympic, named for the Seoul Games. It adds realism by letting you choose a country to represent. Events include fencing, triple jump, freestyle swimming, high dive, clay pigeon shooting, hammer throw, taekwondo, pole vault, canoeing, archery, hurdles and horizontal bar, with hang gliding as a bonus between rounds. Several return from Hyper Sports and the original Track & Field. It topped Famitsu's sales chart. In the Japanese version, arm wrestling can be played against the computer in exhibition, and the gun-firing bonus event of the North American release isn't included.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Sports events are visual; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Track & Field II (1989).
japanese_version_notes: Arm wrestling is available against the computer in exhibition, and there's no gun-firing bonus event (both differ from the NES version).

gameplay_summary: Kung fu action against jiangshi: as a Taoist master, fight through eight towns of hopping vampires and their bosses, learning moves and using items, to reach a final witch.
dossier: Pony Canyon's game of the 1985 Hong Kong hit Mr. Vampire (Reigen Doushi in Japan), the film that started Japan's jiangshi craze. You play a kung fu master who works through eight towns overrun by kyonshi, each with its own boss, before the final showdown with an evil witch. There are a few items and a large selection of fighting moves. The inventory screen lists every item in the game, not just the ones you have. A hidden baby kyonshi character makes the game much harder. Continues are unlimited. The NES Phantom Fighter dropped the film tie-in.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Fighting is visual, but town and item text is Japanese; how much it guides progress isn't documented.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Phantom Fighter (1990).
japanese_version_notes: Licensed from the film Mr. Vampire; the NES version isn't presented as a film tie-in.

gameplay_summary: Command-select occult adventure with RPG battles: as the exorcist monk Kujaku, work through eight chapters against the Iwato god clan and the Dark Lord, fighting random and boss encounters through menus.
dossier: Pony Canyon's game of Makoto Ogino's occult manga, developed by Graphic Research. Its story follows the OVA Kikansai: the exorcist Kujaku begins by fighting the Iwato divine clan and ends up facing the Lord of Darkness. It's a standard command-select adventure, but it adds RPG battle parts, with random encounters and boss fights, all run through menus. Unlike the Sega Mark III version released days later, it has no action sections. There are eight chapters and a password save. The main theme is by Toshihiko Takamizawa of the rock band THE ALFEE. Producer Kazuhiko Arimoto later made Sokoban for Game Boy.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A text-driven command adventure; all play, battles included, is through Japanese menus and dialogue.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Child-oriented silly sports event game starring Donald Duck, loosely ported from the British computer game Alternative World Games.
dossier: Kemco's Famicom sports game starring Disney's Donald Duck. It's a loose port of Gremlin Graphics' 1987 British computer game Alternative World Games, the only Gremlin game Kemco's console deal brought back to the West. That happened as Snoopy's Silly Sports Spectacular, with Donald's graphics replaced by Snoopy and the Peanuts gang. Its events are comic takes on sports, aimed at children. Two of its music tracks, including the menu theme, were reused from Kemco's Famicom Spy vs. Spy II. The sources don't list the individual events.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Simple sports events with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Snoopy's Silly Sports Spectacular (1990).
japanese_version_notes: Stars Disney's Donald Duck; the NES version replaces him with Snoopy and the Peanuts characters.

gameplay_summary: Stage-select action platformer: fight through eight castles with a swordsman and a falcon partner (controllable by a second player), each boss vulnerable to only one sword, so the stage order matters.
dossier: Thinking Rabbit's action game for SETA. Seven of its eight castles can be tackled in any order, but each boss can only be hurt by one sword, earned from another stage, so finding the right route is part of the game. The hero fights with a falcon companion, which a second player can control. Kenzou Kumei's soundtrack gives each stage three pieces of music. The Japanese version has a very different setting from the post-apocalyptic NES story. In the late 19th-century Balkans, a demon-worshipping bandit, Ruth Grandier, has massacred a British Museum expedition and stolen artifacts for a resurrection ritual. Sir Julian James Bond, England's greatest swordsman, is sent with his eagle Cutlass to stop her.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action platforming; the story is not needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as 8 Eyes by Taxan (1990) rather than SETA, with a rewritten story and setting.
japanese_version_notes: The Japanese story is set in the Victorian-era Balkans, with Sir Julian James Bond and his eagle Cutlass against Ruth Grandier's demon cult; the NES version reframes it as Orin the Falconer in a post-nuclear future.

gameplay_summary: Two-player simultaneous command adventure: twins Erika and Satoru explore a whimsical animal world for the Time Crown on a split map, entering locations separately or together, with quizzes and two-player mini-games.
dossier: Namco's fairy-tale adventure, developed by Atlus, and a rare adventure game playable by two people at once. A cat-like being sends the twins Erika and Satoru after the Time Crown, which can alter time and space, in a strange land of animals with place names that pun on Japanese cities. The map is split between the two. Either can enter a building for a close-up while the other keeps moving, and items and flags are shared immediately. There are character touches, like Erika drowning if left idle while swimming until Satoru rescues her. Mini-games are a quiz in one-player and co-op events in two-player, and failing the animal quiz sends you back to the start. The cartridge uses Namco's 163 sound chip with all eight channels. It's also infamous for a crude hidden developer message at the end.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — An adventure built on Japanese dialogue and quizzes; the quiz in particular needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: The cartridge uses Namco's 163 expansion sound chip.

gameplay_summary: Licensed driving action: drive KITT city to city across fifteen missions from Los Angeles and back, shooting enemy cars with lasers and missiles and upgrading fuel, shields and speed.
dossier: Pack-In-Video's game of the TV series, which it follows only loosely. Driving KITT, you take on fifteen city-to-city legs, starting from Los Angeles to San Francisco and ending back in LA. Between missions KITT can be upgraded with more fuel and shield capacity, a higher top speed, and more lasers and missiles to start with. In the first six missions, allied Knight trucks hand out power-ups. ja.wikipedia classes it as a racing game.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Driving and shooting; upgrade menus are simple.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Knight Rider, published in North America by Acclaim (1989) rather than Pack-In-Video.

gameplay_summary: Casino game: start with $700 and play keno, blackjack, roulette and slots in a story mode with random encounters with other characters, or in straight gaming mode.
dossier: HAL Laboratory's casino game, published in Japan by Epic/Sony Records. Unusually, the Japanese Famicom version is in English. After an opening flight into Las Vegas, you choose 'Vegas Dream', a story mode, or 'One Spot', gambling only. You start with $700 at the Epic Palace hotel (renamed the HAL Palace in the American release) and play keno, blackjack, roulette or slots. In story mode, random social encounters with businesspeople, other gamblers and casino staff pop up between rounds. A Super NES sequel, Vegas Stakes, followed.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — The Japanese release is already in English.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Vegas Dream (1990).
japanese_version_notes: In English despite being a Japanese release; the casino is the Epic Palace (the NES version's HAL Palace).

gameplay_summary: Modern hex-based wargame: build and deploy armies of modern weapons across thirty maps, capturing cities and factories to defeat the enemy.
dossier: Bothtec's Famicom port of SystemSoft's 1985 computer wargame Daisenryaku, the start of one of Japan's longest-running strategy series. It's based on the 8-bit computer versions but considerably simplified to fit the Famicom, and it includes thirty maps. The music is by Hitoshi Sakimoto, with sound programming by Masaharu Iwata. Like the rest of the series, it's a turn-based modern war game where capturing cities and factories feeds your production. It scored modestly (22/40) in Famitsu.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A menu-driven wargame with Japanese unit names and commands.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Data-updated edition of Best Play Pro Baseball: the same manager-perspective pennant simulation with player data refreshed to mid-1988.
dossier: ASCII's October 1988 refresh of Best Play Pro Baseball, the strategy-focused baseball sim by Hiroyuki Sonobe (later of Derby Stallion). The original sold out its small first shipment, and this edition carries player data as of summer 1988. The game is unchanged. You play the manager, calling pinch hitters, relief changes, steals and defensive shifts through a pennant race, or let the computer run teams. Starting pitchers rotate on a stamina model. Player names and S-to-E ratings can be freely edited, and it supports the Turbo File. Some game guides omit this edition entirely.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A management simulation run through Japanese menus, standings and player data.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: Supports ASCII's Turbo File for external save data.

gameplay_summary: Tournament bass fishing: cast from an overhead view with a power meter, work lures to hook bass, and catch enough heavy fish each day to advance through tournaments at four lakes.
dossier: Hot-B's sequel to its MSX and Famicom The Black Bass, and the first in the series released abroad (as The Black Bass, with 'The Black Bass USA' on the title screen). You advance through bass tournaments at four lakes. Each runs from sunrise to sunset, and you only move on if your catch is big enough in number and average weight. Pike and rainbow and brown trout also bite but don't count. Casting is from an overhead view, with the strength set by a power meter at the bottom of the screen.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Fishing is visual; menus are simple.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as The Black Bass (1989).

gameplay_summary: Free-scrolling helicopter shooter: fly an armoured gunship through enemy territory destroying tanks, guns and boats, rescuing all the hostages in each stage, and landing at certain spots to upgrade.
dossier: Data East's home version of its 1988 arcade helicopter shooter. The arcade game is an auto-scrolling horizontal shooter across six missions in Southeast Asia, from Sumatra to the enemy HQ. The home version stops the automatic scrolling and becomes something closer to Choplifter: you fly freely, and the goal of each stage is to rescue every hostage while fighting tanks, cannons, submarines and gunboats. Landing in certain places upgrades the helicopter. It's the same game Data East released on the NES.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Shooting action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Cobra Command (North America 1988).

gameplay_summary: Board-game-style RPG adaptation of Namco's arcade Genpei Touma Den, themed on the resurrected Taira no Kagekiyo's quest against Minamoto no Yoritomo; the sources give no detail of the board system.
dossier: Namco didn't port its 1986 arcade action game to the Famicom; it changed genre and released this board-game-style computer RPG on the same theme. The arcade original, based on a joruri play, has the samurai Taira no Kagekiyo, killed at Dan-no-ura, resurrected to collect the three sacred treasures and march on Kamakura to kill Yoritomo, fighting Yoshitsune and Benkei along the way. It's known for its painterly Japanese style. The ja.wikipedia article covers the arcade game in detail but says little about how this board game plays, so its board, battles and win conditions are unconfirmed.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A board-game RPG with Japanese text events and menus; not detailed in sources.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling platformer: as Mario or Luigi, cross eight themed worlds on a map with branching paths, use power-ups like the Super Leaf and Tanooki Suit to fly, and rescue Princess Toadstool and the rulers of seven kingdoms from Bowser.
dossier: Nintendo's third Super Mario Bros., directed by Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka, and a Famitsu Platinum Hall of Fame game. Bowser has thrown seven kingdoms into chaos and taken Princess Toadstool, and Mario and Luigi head out across eight worlds on an overworld map with branching paths, Toad Houses and spade-panel bonus games. New moves include sliding down slopes, carrying and throwing shells and blocks, and climbing vines. New power-ups like the Super Leaf and Tanooki Suit let Mario fly and float. The difficulty is gentle early and climbs steadily, far from Super Mario Bros. 2's (The Lost Levels') harshness.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Platforming with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Super Mario Bros. 3 (North America 1990).

gameplay_summary: Presidential campaign sim: choose liberal, conservative or centrist positions on four issues, then manage funds and campaign from the February primaries through the party convention to November's general election.
dossier: Hect's election sim, released just before the 1988 US presidential election and loosely based on it, with characters modelled on real candidates and politicians. It was conceived and directed by Shintaro Ito, then a Japanese CNN Daywatch newscaster and later a politician himself. You start by taking liberal, conservative or centrist positions on four issues. Liberal stances alienate religious voters, conservative ones put off students and the working class, and centrism, trying to please everyone, pleases no one. From February primaries through the convention to November, you spend your funds carefully without going bankrupt. Famitsu reviewers were split: some found it educational and approachable, others said the system meant little to Japanese children.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A text-heavy political simulation in Japanese about the US electoral system.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Grand strategy in late Han China: as a warlord, govern provinces, manage officers, economy and armies, and use diplomacy, intrigue and war to unify the land.
dossier: Koei's Famicom port of the first Sangokushi (1985), the start of its Romance of the Three Kingdoms series. Producer is Kou Shibusawa and the music is by Yoko Kanno. Based on the classic novel, it has you take a warlord from the Three Kingdoms era and unify China. Unlike Nobunaga's Ambition, it features unclaimed territory and a system of subordinate officers serving under you. You govern your provinces and build armies. Western critics praised the computer original for economics, bribery, covert action and diplomacy offering many routes to victory beyond conquest. The NES release translated it into English.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Menu-heavy strategy with Japanese commands, officer names and reports.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Romance of the Three Kingdoms (1989).

gameplay_summary: Absurdist command adventure: switch between student time-traveller Bunroku and Marco Polo, using commands like look, talk, punch and take, as they travel from 1275 Venice across Asia to Kublai Khan and on to Zipangu.
dossier: Natsume's first game, from a studio founded by former Konami developers. The title puns on Marco Polo's Travels, but it's actually the name of the hero, Bunroku Touhouken, a time-travel engineering student whose dream is the best general store in Daikanyama. Sure that Japan was the golden Zipangu, he packs cheap Akihabara goods and time-travels to 1275 Venice, and an accident sweeps him onto Marco Polo's journey. Like Nintendo's Famicom Mukashibanashi adventures, you switch between characters using eight commands, including 'punch'. Billed as a 'New Wave Psychedelic Adventure', it's a deranged black comedy whose outrageous lines have been called unreleasable today. The password uses symbols like haniwa, eyeballs and planaria, set to a Maim Maim arrangement.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — The game is its absurd Japanese script; without reading, the comedy and the solutions are lost.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Overhead American football: pick one of twelve teams and play free-scrolling vertical football with a range of formations, against the computer or a second player.
dossier: K Amusement's Famicom port of SNK's 1987 arcade football game, which resembled Irem's 10-Yard Fight but used SNK's rotary joystick for aiming passes and blocking. On the Famicom it's played on a horizontal screen with vertical, eight-way scrolling. You choose one of twelve teams and can play the computer or another player. It covers most official rules and the major running and passing plays, along with field goals and punts. The American NES release, by SNK, limits human players to five basic plays (long pass, short pass, QB sneak, hand-off, punt or field goal); the Famicom version's play set isn't separately documented.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Football is visual; play selection is simple.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Touchdown Fever (1991).
